description.text: Stamford, an acquaintance of Watson's from Bart's Hospital, introduces Watson to Sherlock Holmes in the chemical laboratory at St. Bartholomew's Hospital. Holmes immediately deduces that Watson has been in Afghanistan. Both men are looking for lodgings; Stamford suggests they might share rooms.
This meeting sets in motion the entire Holmes canon — without it, there is no narrator, no partnership, and no published accounts.
At the Battle of Maiwand during the Second Anglo-Afghan War, Watson — serving as an assistant surgeon attached to the Berkshires — is struck by a Jezail bullet.

The wound's location is described inconsistently across the canon (shoulder in A Study in Scarlet, leg in The Sign of the Four), generating one of the longest-running debates in Sherlockian scholarship.

His orderly Murray brings him out of the Ghazi attack. Watson contracts enteric fever during recovery and is invalided home to England, arriving in London with no friends, no family, and a wound pension of eleven shillings and sixpence a day. The injury is the proximate cause of his meeting Holmes — without it he would have remained on military duty rather than seeking cheap shared lodgings in London. Periodically referenced through the canon when Watson's old wound aches in damp weather.

name: Holmes Outwitted by Irene Adler
description: Hired by the King of Bohemia to recover a compromising photograph from his former lover Irene Adler, Holmes disguises himself first as a groom and then as a Nonconformist clergyman, stages a false fire at Briony Lodge to provoke Adler into revealing the photograph's hiding place, and returns the next morning to retrieve it — only to find Adler has recognised him despite his disguise, departed England with her new husband, and left a letter of farewell. The photograph remains in her possession. Holmes asks the King for one of Adler's photographs as his sole reward. From this point onward Holmes refers to her always as "the woman" — the only person in the canon ever to defeat him decisively.

name: Watson Meets Mycroft Holmes
description: In The Greek Interpreter, Holmes casually mentions his elder brother Mycroft for the first time. Watson, after seven years' acquaintance, has assumed Holmes had no living relatives. Holmes takes Watson to the Diogenes Club — the strangest club in London, whose members are forbidden to converse — and introduces him to Mycroft. Mycroft demonstrates deductive faculties superior to Sherlock's (according to Sherlock himself), explaining that he lacks the energy and ambition to apply them to detective work, instead serving the British Government in a capacity Watson does not fully understand until much later. Mycroft becomes a recurring figure in subsequent stories.

name: The Reichenbach Falls Confrontation
description: At the Reichenbach Falls near Meiringen, Switzerland, Sherlock Holmes and Professor Moriarty engage in a final struggle at the edge of the precipice. Holmes has dismantled Moriarty's criminal network and both men know there can be only one outcome. Holmes sends Watson away on a false errand. When Watson returns, both men are gone — only footprints leading to the edge and Holmes's farewell note remain. Witnesses report seeing two men struggling. The world believes both dead. Holmes later reveals he survived using Baritsu, throwing Moriarty while clinging to the cliff face. He spent three years traveling under the alias Sigerson.

name: The Great Hiatus (Holmes's Missing Years)
description: After his apparent death at Reichenbach, Holmes spends three years travelling under the alias Sigerson. By his own account in The Empty House, he visits Tibet (where he spends two years and meets the head Lama at Lhasa), passes through Persia, looks in at Mecca, pays a brief visit to the Khalifa at Khartoum, and finally settles for several months in research at Montpellier in the south of France studying coal-tar derivatives. Throughout the Hiatus, only Mycroft knows Holmes is alive; Mycroft maintains the rooms at Baker Street and supplies Holmes with money. The Hiatus ends when news reaches Holmes that the last remnants of Moriarty's network — chiefly Colonel Moran — can finally be neutralised. The period has generated more Sherlockian apocrypha than any other gap in the canon.

name: Watson and Mary Morstan's Marriage
description: At the conclusion of The Sign of the Four, Watson proposes to Mary Morstan once it becomes clear the Agra treasure has been lost — preserving his honour by waiting until she is no longer an heiress. Their marriage takes place shortly thereafter (the canon does not give an exact date; scholarship places it late 1888 or early 1889). Watson moves out of 221B Baker Street to establish his own medical practice in Paddington. The marriage explains his intermittent availability across the Adventures and Memoirs era — Watson visits Holmes when his practice is slow, and Mary's mild patience with the relationship is alluded to in passing. Holmes notes the loss of his Boswell with characteristic restraint.

name: Mary Morstan's Death
description: Mary Morstan dies during the period of Holmes's apparent death — between The Final Problem (May 1891) and The Empty House (April 1894). Watson refers to "my own sad bereavement" in the opening of The Empty House but provides no details, and the event is never directly depicted. Her death restores Watson to his bachelor state and explains his return to shared lodgings at 221B Baker Street upon Holmes's reappearance. Sherlockian scholarship has speculated extensively about cause and date; the canon offers nothing.

name: The Capture of Colonel Sebastian Moran
description: On the night of his return to London, Holmes enacts a long-planned trap. He places a wax bust of himself in the lit window of 221B Baker Street, visible from the street, then conceals himself with Watson in the empty Camden House across the way. Colonel Moran — the second most dangerous man in London, the executor of Moriarty's surviving organisation, and the assassin Holmes has been hunting since the Hiatus — takes the bait. He fires a soft revolver bullet from a specially modified von Herder air gun through the window into the bust. Holmes and Lestrade arrest him on the spot. Moran's capture closes the Moriarty business and makes London safe for Holmes's return.

name: The Death of Charles Augustus Milverton
description: Holmes, hired by a society lady to recover compromising letters from the blackmailer Milverton, infiltrates Appledore Towers with Watson. While they hide in the study planning to crack Milverton's safe, an unidentified woman arrives — one of Milverton's previous victims, whose husband had died of grief over letters Milverton sold — and shoots Milverton dead. Holmes and Watson watch from concealment without intervening. They burn Milverton's blackmail archive and escape. The next day, Lestrade asks for Holmes's help identifying the killer; Holmes refuses. The case is one of the few in which Holmes condones (and conceals) a murder, and his refusal is presented without ambiguity as morally correct.

name: Holmes's Return to London
description: Three years after the Reichenbach Falls, Sherlock Holmes returns to London, revealing himself to Watson in disguise before disclosing his identity. Holmes explains he has spent three years traveling as Sigerson — through Tibet (visiting the head lama at Lhasa), Persia, Mecca, and France — waiting until enough of Moriarty's surviving network had been captured or scattered to make his return safe. Watson faints upon the revelation. Holmes's immediate purpose in returning is to deal with Colonel Sebastian Moran, the last significant threat remaining from Moriarty's organization.

name: Holmes's Retirement to the Sussex Downs

description.text: At some point in 1903 Holmes retires from active practice and moves to a small farm on the Sussex Downs near Eastbourne, devoting himself to bee-keeping and the writing of his Practical Handbook of Bee Culture. The Preface to His Last Bow, written by Watson, confirms the retirement.

The Adventure of the Lion's Mane (narrated by Holmes himself) describes his Sussex life directly. Holmes consents to be drawn back into active work twice — for the Von Bork affair in 1914, and for the Lion's Mane investigation in his own neighbourhood.
The retirement permanently changes the geography and tone of the late canon.

name: Holmes's Counter-Espionage Service in 1914
description: On the eve of the First World War, Holmes — drawn out of retirement two years earlier by the Foreign Minister and the Premier — completes a long undercover operation against the German agent Von Bork. Posing as the Irish-American spy "Altamont," Holmes has spent two years infiltrating Von Bork's espionage network in England, collecting and corrupting intelligence. He arrests Von Bork on the eve of his planned escape to Germany, hands his apparently sealed dispatches over to British intelligence, and reunites briefly with Watson — who is driving the car. Holmes is then sixty years old. The story is the last canonical chronological appearance of Holmes; the famous "east wind coming, Watson" speech places his career in elegiac context.
